intro: Fourteen verses on how short a life is, spoken by someone who decided not to speak. The psalm opens with a vow of silence kept in front of an enemy, records what that silence did to the speaker, and then breaks it. What comes out is not the complaint he was holding in but a request to be told the length of his own days. The word for breath or vapour, the one that runs through Ecclesiastes, appears three times, and the psalm ends without a resolution: the last line asks God to look away. It is addressed to Jeduthun, one of the Levites David appointed over the music.

stichs.en: For the director, for Jeduthun.
A psalm of David.

verses.summary: Two prepositional phrases with the same prefix, one naming an office and one a person. Jeduthun heads two other psalms, which suggests a repertoire rather than a single occasion.

stichs.en: I said: let me guard my ways from sinning with my tongue;
let me keep a muzzle on my mouth,
as long as the wicked man is in front of me.

verses.summary: The psalm begins with a quotation of a decision already taken. Both cohortatives use the same verb, to guard, and the object shifts from ways to mouth, so the whole discipline of life narrows down to speech.

stichs.en: I was struck dumb, silent;
I kept quiet, even from good,
and my pain was stirred up.

verses.summary: The vow works and costs. Holding back from saying anything bad meant holding back from saying anything at all, and the pain that had no exit turned inward instead of dissolving.

stichs.en: My heart grew hot inside me;
as I brooded, a fire burned.
Then I spoke with my tongue:

verses.summary: The silence breaks, and the last two words undo the vow of verse 2 in its own vocabulary: the tongue he swore not to sin with is the one he now uses. Everything from here to verse 14 is the speech.

stichs.en: LORD, let me know my end,
and the measure of my days, whatever it is;
let me know how fleeting I am.

verses.summary: After all that pressure, the request is for information, not relief. He asks for the number, which is the one thing that would make the complaint unnecessary or unbearable.

stichs.en: Look, You have made my days a few handbreadths,
and my lifetime is as nothing in front of You.
Every man, however firmly he stands, is only a breath.
Selah.

verses.summary: The answer arrives inside the question. A handbreadth is the smallest unit measured on the body, and the comparison is not to a long time but to nothing at all, which is a different kind of statement.

stichs.en: A man walks about as a mere image;
for a breath they are in uproar.
He piles things up and does not know who will gather them in.

verses.summary: Three pictures of futility: a man who is only an appearance, a crowd making noise over nothing, and a saver whose heir is unknown. The last one is the argument Ecclesiastes makes at length.

stichs.en: And now, my Lord, what am I waiting for?
My hope is in You.

verses.summary: The turn of the psalm, and the only verse in it that says something positive without immediately taking it back. The question and the answer sit in the same breath: nothing is worth waiting for, therefore You are.

stichs.en: Rescue me from all my rebellions;
do not make me the taunt of the fool.

verses.summary: The first thing asked for after the hope is stated is not longer life but cleaning up. The wicked man of verse 2, watched in silence, comes back here as someone who would use the speaker's failure as material.

stichs.en: I am struck dumb, I do not open my mouth,
because it is You who did this.

verses.summary: The same verb as verse 3, and a completely different silence. The first was a policy adopted against an enemy; this one is what is left once the source of the trouble has been identified.

stichs.en: Take Your blow off me;
under the attack of Your hand I am finished.

verses.summary: Silence lasted one verse. The request is addressed to the same hand that is doing the striking, which is the position the whole psalm is written from.

stichs.en: With rebukes for guilt You discipline a man,
and like a moth You dissolve what he treasures.
Every man is only a breath.
Selah.

verses.summary: The refrain from verse 6 returns, shortened. The moth does not attack the man, it eats the thing he loves, so the discipline described works by removing what was accumulated in verse 7.

stichs.en: Hear my prayer, LORD,
give ear to my cry for help,
do not stay deaf to my tears;
for I am a stranger with You, a settler like all my fathers.

verses.summary: Three imperatives escalating from prayer to cry to tears, then the ground of the request. The two nouns at the end are the legal terms for someone living on land that is not his.

stichs.en: Look away from me and let me get my breath back,
before I go and am no more.

verses.summary: The psalm ends by asking for the opposite of what psalms usually ask for. Attention has been the problem throughout, so the last request is to be left alone long enough to breathe.

pardes.body: A vow, its cost, its collapse, and what came out. Verses 2 to 4 narrate: I decided to say nothing while the wicked man was watching, I said nothing, it burned, I spoke. Verses 5 to 14 are the speech, and it is not the complaint that was being held back. It asks for the length of a life, gets an answer that is worse than the question, and turns into a request first for forgiveness and then for distance. The refrain about every man being a breath lands twice, at {{6.9}} and {{12.9}}, with a third instance inside verse 7 at {{7.5}}. Nothing is resolved. The final word at {{14.5}} is a negation of existence, and the psalm stops there.

The word at {{7.1}} is the one used in Genesis for the image in which humanity was made, and here it stands for something insubstantial that a man walks around as. Translators split over it: some keep the sense of image or semblance, others read it as a shadow or phantom, and the choice changes whether the line is about being a copy or about being unreal. The verb at {{3.0}} and {{10.0}} is the same in both places, from the root for being mute, and it holds the psalm's two silences together. Two other words are worth stopping on: {{2.7}}, a muzzle, which is an object put on an animal, and {{5.9}}, a rare adjective from the root meaning to cease, so the speaker asks not how long he will live but how much of a stopping he already is.

The claim at {{13.10}} and {{13.13}}, that the speaker is a stranger and a settler with God, has two anchors elsewhere in the Bible. Leviticus 25 gives the reason the land cannot be sold permanently, that the people are strangers and settlers with God, who owns it; and in 1 Chronicles 29 David uses the same pair of words in prayer, saying that we are strangers before You and settlers like all our fathers. Read against those, the line is not self-pity. It is a legal argument: a resident alien has no property claim but does have a claim on the protection of the householder, and the request that follows is exactly what a tenant may ask. The tears of the same verse are treated in the same register, as something submitted rather than merely shed.

The mystical readings take the last verse as the hard one, because asking God to look away is the reverse of every other prayer in the book. One line of reading treats the psalm as a description of a soul under a scrutiny it cannot survive, where the withdrawal asked for is the concealment that makes a limited creature able to exist at all, and the request is therefore not for abandonment but for a measured distance. The word at {{14.0}}, look away, and the word for the stranger at {{13.10}} then belong together: the guest lives by the host's restraint. The three occurrences of breath are read the same way, less as a verdict on human worth than as a description of what a thing made of breath needs from what made it.
